review_status: DRAFT - conservative triage rules authored from general, widely published cattle-health guidance. NOT yet reviewed or validated by a veterinarian. Must be reviewed before any real-world reliance.

rules.concern: Possible notifiable disease with sudden death (for example anthrax)
rules.why: Sudden death or bleeding from body openings can be caused by serious infectious diseases that are dangerous to people and other animals.
next_steps: Do NOT open, skin or move any carcass
Keep people and other animals away from the animal and the area
Contact your veterinary officer or county veterinary office immediately
Wash hands thoroughly and avoid contact with blood or discharges

rules.concern: Bloat (gas build-up in the rumen) with breathing difficulty
rules.why: A swollen left flank with breathing trouble can become life-threatening within hours.
next_steps: Call a veterinarian or animal health worker immediately
Keep the animal calm and on its feet if possible
Remove access to lush legume pasture, wet grass or grain
Do not give home remedies or oils without veterinary instruction

rules.concern: Bloat (gas build-up in the rumen)
rules.why: A swollen left side after feeding can indicate bloat or other digestive problems.
next_steps: Contact a veterinarian or animal health worker today
Remove access to lush legume pasture, wet grass or grain
Watch breathing closely; if it becomes laboured treat as an emergency

rules.concern: Cow unable to rise after calving (for example low blood calcium or other metabolic/obstetric problem)
rules.why: A cow that cannot stand around calving needs prompt professional assessment; several causes need different treatment.
next_steps: Call a veterinarian immediately
Provide shade, shelter and soft, non-slip bedding; help the cow rest upright on her chest if she can
Do not force liquids into a cow that cannot swallow properly (risk of choking/aspiration)

rules.concern: Nervous-system signs (many causes, including some serious infections such as rabies)
rules.why: Staggering, circling, tremors or seizures can have many serious causes, some of which are dangerous to people.
next_steps: Call a veterinarian immediately
Avoid touching the animal's saliva or mouth; wear gloves for any necessary handling
If you were bitten or saliva touched broken skin, wash the area well with soap and water and seek medical care
Keep other animals and children away

rules.concern: Pattern that can occur with foot-and-mouth disease (a notifiable disease)
rules.why: Mouth sores together with drooling, foot lesions or lameness can occur with foot-and-mouth disease, which spreads very easily.
next_steps: Isolate the animal and stop all animal movement on and off the farm
Report to your veterinary officer or county veterinary office immediately
Clean and disinfect boots, clothing and equipment before visiting other animals or farms
Do not sell or move animals or milk until a veterinarian advises

rules.concern: Pattern that can occur with lumpy skin disease (a notifiable disease in many areas)
rules.why: Firm skin lumps with fever or swollen lymph nodes can occur with lumpy skin disease, which is spread by biting insects and animal movement.
next_steps: Isolate the animal from the herd
Report to your veterinary officer or county veterinary office
Reduce biting-fly exposure (shelter, clean up manure and standing water)
Do not move animals until a veterinarian advises

rules.concern: Pattern that can occur with blackleg (a rapidly fatal clostridial disease, mainly in young cattle)
rules.why: A hot, painful swelling over a muscle with lameness or fever can progress very quickly.
next_steps: Call a veterinarian immediately
Do not cut into the swelling
Ask the veterinarian about vaccination for the rest of the herd

rules.concern: Possible tick-borne disease (for example East Coast fever)
rules.why: Fever with swollen lymph nodes and ticks is a common pattern in tick-borne diseases, which can be fatal if treatment is delayed.
next_steps: Contact a veterinarian or animal health worker today for a proper diagnosis
Provide shade and clean water
Ask about a tick-control programme for the herd

rules.concern: Possible blood-parasite disease (for example babesiosis or anaplasmosis) or other cause of anaemia
rules.why: Red-brown urine or pale gums with fever or ticks can mean red blood cells are being destroyed.
next_steps: Contact a veterinarian today
Keep the animal quiet, shaded and with water; avoid stressing or running it

rules.concern: Serious respiratory problem (for example pneumonia)
rules.why: Laboured breathing with cough, nasal discharge or fever suggests a significant chest infection.
next_steps: Contact a veterinarian today
Provide shade, ventilation without draughts, and clean water
Separate the animal from the herd
Do not exercise or transport the animal unless advised

rules.concern: Respiratory infection
rules.why: Cough, nasal discharge or fast breathing can be an early sign of respiratory disease, heat stress or dusty/poorly ventilated housing.
next_steps: Arrange a veterinary or animal-health-worker visit within a day or two
Improve ventilation and reduce dust
Check body temperature if you have a thermometer
Separate the animal if others are affected

rules.concern: Severe mastitis (udder infection) with whole-body illness

in: Very weak or lying down and not getting up

rules.why: A hard or abnormal udder with fever, poor appetite or weakness can indicate severe mastitis.
next_steps: Contact a veterinarian today
Milk out the affected quarter(s) frequently as the veterinarian advises
Milk this cow last and keep her milk out of the supply; ask the veterinarian about milk withholding
Keep bedding clean and dry

rules.concern: Possible mastitis (udder infection)
rules.why: Swelling, heat or clots/watery/bloody milk are common signs of mastitis.
next_steps: Arrange a veterinary or animal-health-worker visit within a day
Do a strip-cup check of each quarter and note which quarter is affected
Milk this cow last, with clean hands and equipment, and keep her milk out of the supply until advised
Keep bedding clean and dry

rules.concern: Calf diarrhoea with risk of dehydration
rules.why: Calves can become dangerously dehydrated within a day of diarrhoea starting.
next_steps: Contact a veterinarian or animal health worker today
Keep the calf warm, dry and with access to clean water
Ask the veterinarian how to give oral rehydration safely and whether milk feeding should change
Wash hands after handling; some causes can infect people

rules.concern: Bloody diarrhoea (for example parasites such as coccidiosis, or an infection)
rules.why: Blood in the dung needs a proper diagnosis because causes and treatments differ.
next_steps: Contact a veterinarian today
Keep the animal separate, with clean water
Collect a fresh dung sample if the veterinarian asks for one

rules.concern: Diarrhoea (diet, parasites or infection)
rules.why: Diarrhoea can come from feed changes, worms, or infections.
next_steps: Arrange a veterinary or animal-health-worker visit within a day or two
Provide clean water and avoid sudden feed changes
Note how many animals are affected

rules.concern: Abortion, retained placenta or abnormal discharge (possible infectious cause)
rules.why: Abortions and uterine discharge can be caused by infections, including some that can infect people (for example brucellosis).
next_steps: Contact a veterinarian today
Wear gloves and wash well after handling any discharge, foetus or placenta; keep children away
Isolate the cow and keep any aborted material for the veterinarian rather than burying it
Do not drink raw milk from the animal until a veterinarian advises

rules.concern: High fever (many possible infectious causes)
rules.why: A temperature of 40.5 C or more is a significant fever.
next_steps: Contact a veterinarian today
Provide shade and clean water; avoid exercising the animal
Record temperature again in a few hours

rules.concern: Low body temperature (possible collapse, shock or severe illness)
rules.why: A very low temperature in a sick animal can indicate collapse, shock or metabolic emergencies.
next_steps: Call a veterinarian immediately
Keep the animal warm, dry and out of wind

rules.concern: Fever (many possible causes)
rules.why: A temperature of 39.5 C or more is above the normal range for adult cattle.
next_steps: Arrange a veterinary or animal-health-worker visit within a day
Provide shade and clean water
Recheck the temperature in a few hours

rules.concern: Not eating or chewing cud (digestive or whole-body illness)

in: Very weak or lying down and not getting up

rules.why: A cow that is dull and not eating or chewing cud may have a digestive or whole-body illness.
next_steps: Contact a veterinarian today
Provide clean water and avoid forcing feed
Record milk drop, dung and temperature if you can

rules.concern: Very weak or unable to rise

in: Very weak or lying down and not getting up

rules.why: An animal that cannot rise is in a serious condition whatever the cause.
next_steps: Call a veterinarian immediately
Provide shade, shelter, water within reach and soft bedding
Turn the animal regularly if advised

rules.concern: Swollen joint in a calf (possible joint infection)
rules.why: Joint infections in calves can cause permanent damage if not treated promptly.
next_steps: Contact a veterinarian today
Keep the calf on clean, dry bedding

rules.concern: Lameness (hoof problem, injury or joint problem)
rules.why: Lameness is commonly caused by hoof infections, injury or joint problems.
next_steps: Arrange a hoof check by a veterinarian or trained hoof trimmer within a few days
Keep the animal on soft, dry ground
Check for stones, wounds or swelling between the hooves

rules.concern: Eye infection (for example pinkeye)
rules.why: Watery or pus-like eye discharge, squinting or cloudiness may be pinkeye or an injury, and spreads through flies and contact.
next_steps: Arrange a veterinary or animal-health-worker visit within a day or two
Provide shade to reduce sun irritation
Separate affected animals and control flies

rules.concern: Skin condition (mange, lice, ticks, ringworm or other)
rules.why: Scabs, hair loss, itching or ticks have several possible causes, some of which can spread to other animals or people (for example ringworm).
next_steps: Ask a veterinarian or animal health worker to identify the cause
Wear gloves and wash hands after handling affected animals
Ask about a tick- and parasite-control programme for the herd

rules.concern: Weight loss or poor condition (parasites, nutrition or chronic disease)
rules.why: Unexplained weight loss can have many causes including worms, poor diet, and chronic infections.
next_steps: Arrange a veterinary check and ask about a dung test for worms
Review feed quality, quantity and mineral supply
Record body condition and weigh/measure regularly

general_steps: Provide shade, clean water and a calm environment.
Keep sick animals apart from the healthy herd when the cause is unknown.
Wear gloves and wash hands after handling sick animals.
Write down what you see, when it started, and your animal's temperature so the veterinarian has accurate information.
Do not give antibiotics, dewormers or other medicines unless a veterinarian or qualified animal health worker prescribes them.
